title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 98
paragraphs: The Greeks, however, when informed that the barbarians had gone off to the mainland, were vexed, thinking they had escaped, and were at a loss what to do — whether to go back home or to sail down toward the Hellespont. At last they resolved to do neither, but to sail on to the mainland. Having prepared for a sea-fight both boarding bridges and everything else required, they sailed toward Mycale; and when they came near the camp, no one was seen putting out against them, but they perceived ships drawn up within the wall and a large land-army ranged along the shore. Then first Leotychides, sailing along in his ship and coming as near the shore as he could, made proclamation by a herald to the Ionians, saying: “Ionians, those of you who chance to be within earshot, attend to what I say — for the Persians will understand nothing of what I enjoin to you. When we join battle, let every one of you remember first the freedom of all, and then the watchword ‘Hebe'; and let him who has not heard this learn it from him who has.” The intent of this act was the same as that of Themistocles at Artemisium: either the words uttered would escape the barbarians' notice and persuade the Ionians, or, if reported to the barbarians, would make them distrustful of the Greeks.
